ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Why conjugation matters

A medical student studies the vaccine that prevents most classic Hib epiglottitis. It links a capsular polysaccharide to a carrier protein. What immunologic advantage is especially important for protecting infants and young children?

  1. Recruitment of T-cell help and immunologic memory
  2. T-cell-independent activation with predominantly short-lived IgM
  3. Passive transfer of preformed antibodies from the vaccine
  4. Selective induction of cytotoxic T cells without antibody production
  5. Suppression of germinal-center formation to limit inflammation
Answer and explanation

Recruitment of T-cell help and immunologic memory

Protein conjugation permits T-cell-dependent responses to the polysaccharide antigen, improving infant responses and memory.

Option explanations

Recruitment of T-cell help and immunologic memory: Protein conjugation permits T-cell-dependent responses to the polysaccharide antigen, improving infant responses and memory.

T-cell-independent activation with predominantly short-lived IgM: Protein conjugation is intended to overcome the limited infant response to unconjugated polysaccharides.

Passive transfer of preformed antibodies from the vaccine: Conjugate vaccines generate active immunity rather than supplying preformed protective immunoglobulin.

Selective induction of cytotoxic T cells without antibody production: Protection against the capsule depends importantly on antibody responses supported by T-cell help.

Suppression of germinal-center formation to limit inflammation: Conjugation supports the immune processes that produce effective antibody and memory rather than suppressing them.
